title: PhasePilot: a closed loop for phase maps

beats.heading: PhasePilot
beats.subtitle: Muse decides, SAM checks, PhaseScan runs
beats.presenter: PhasePilot closes the loop between a microfluidic rig and Muse so each experiment chooses the next one.
Condensates organise the cell through protein phase separation, and every protein has its own phase diagram to map.

beats.heading: PhaseScan on Beta3
bullets: Beta3 mixes protein, RNA, crowder and buffer on-chip with syringe pumps
The chip stage and pumps run unattended between decisions
Filmed on the real rig in our Cambridge lab
beats.note: Real Beta3 footage shot in the lab today.
beats.presenter: This is PhaseScan, our Beta3 microfluidic rig at Transition Bio, mixing the components on a chip.

beats.heading: Small drops, big maps
bullets: Droplets pass the camera and are imaged in three fluorescence channels
Each droplet is read live as mixed or phase separated
One droplet is 100 pL, ~1,000,000x less protein per data point
beats.note: Every droplet is one experimental condition.
beats.presenter: Each 100 picolitre droplet is a single experiment, using about a million times less protein per data point.
Because every added dimension multiplies the work, we handed the experiment to Muse, with SAM reading droplets and a Bayesian planner sampling where the information is.

beats.heading: Today: live on Beta3
bullets: Live run today: G3BP1 / PolyA RNA / PEG on Beta3, 4 November 2026
Muse chose each setpoint from the live evidence and explained why
SAM outlined every droplet; only passing images count as results
beats.note: The real PhasePilot dashboard during today's live run.
beats.presenter: Today this loop ran live on Beta3 with G3BP1, PolyA RNA and PEG, and Muse explained every setpoint it chose.
The dashboard has four panels: decisions, Muse reasoning, SAM quality control, and results with the phase map.
SAM ViT-B outlines every droplet on real frames, green for accepted and red for rejected, so a result only counts when the image passes.
Here muse-spark-1.3 shows its written reasoning for the next setpoint, readable before the rig moves.
The Bayesian planner redraws the phase map as results land, with the predicted boundary dashed, and sampling follows that boundary.

beats.heading: What the loop saved

stats.line: 20x less protein to map the phase boundary

stats.sub: +2 variables at 4 levels per variable, same time and protein

beats.footnote: Source: 3-variable replay (G3BP1 / TDP-43 / RNA), boundary accuracy at or above 0.997 vs the full scan.
beats.presenter: The replay used twenty times less protein and seventeen times less instrument time, buying at least one extra variable.

beats.heading: Scaling: days, not months
beats.line: At six variables: 36 days vs 2 days
beats.sub: Legacy scan vs PhasePilot in instrument days against variables mapped
beats.green_line: Raster costs k^n; the loop samples the n-1 boundary, ~k^(n-1), buying log_k(17) dimensions.
beats.presenter: At six variables the legacy scan takes thirty-six instrument days while PhasePilot takes two, because it samples the boundary surface.
Biology is high-dimensional across protein, RNA, crowder, salt, pH, compound and temperature, and one closed loop can search any of that space.
